name: Pinar de Chamartín
etymology_summary: Named after a pine grove ('pinar') near the Chamartin area. The pinar belonged to the Duques de Pastrana y del Infantado, who kept their country estate in Chamartin village. When Napoleon arrived on 2 December 1808 to personally direct the second French siege of Madrid, he lodged at one of their palaces. Legend holds that a monumental century-old pine -- 'el Pino de Napoleon' -- stood in the grove where the emperor liked to meditate on strategy; from this rural office he issued his Seven Decrees of 4 December abolishing the Old Regime and the Inquisition. In 1879 the Duques donated the estate 'El Recuerdo' to the Jesuits, who founded the Colegio Nuestra Senora del Recuerdo on the grounds. 'Chamartin' etymology debated: possibly Basque 'ecta-Martin' (village of captain Martin). Interchange with Metro lines 1 and 4.
named_after: Pinar de Chamartín (pine grove near Chamartín area)

name: Fuente de la Mora
etymology_summary: Named after the old Camino Fuente de la Mora, a rural path. 'Fuente' means spring/fountain; 'Mora' is etymologically debated. It may derive from pre-Roman root *mor- meaning 'heap of stones' (per Garcia Sanchez, CVC 2008, discussing related toponyms like Valdemoro), suggesting 'spring among the rocks'. Alternatively, 'mora' could reference a Moorish woman (folk legend) or the mulberry fruit (Latin morum). The site has archaeological significance: a 3rd-2nd century BC Carpetano settlement was excavated nearby. The station was originally planned as 'Manoteras' and is shared with Cercanias line C-1.
named_after: Fuente de la Mora (spring, from pre-Roman mor-: stones)
source: Garcia Sanchez CVC Rinconete Part IV (cvc.cervantes.es/el_rinconete/anteriores/enero_08/28012008_01.htm); comunidad.madrid/cultura/patrimonio-cultural/yacimiento-arqueologico-fuente-mora

name: Virgen del Cortijo
etymology_summary: Named after the Virgen del Cortijo neighbourhood in Hortaleza. In 1966 the city approved the Plan Parcial that created this development on vacant northern land. Built in phases by Pryconsa, the neighbourhood is popularly called 'La Colmena' (the beehive) because its streets and squares form a distinctive hexagonal grid. 'Cortijo' means farmstead, evoking the rural landscape that preceded urbanisation. The station opened in 2007 on ML1.
named_after: Virgen del Cortijo neighbourhood (Virgin Mary of the farmstead)

name: Antonio Saura
etymology_summary: Named after the street honouring Antonio Saura Atares (1930-1998), a major Spanish painter of the post-war period. In 1957 he co-founded the El Paso group in Madrid, a collective of painters, sculptors and critics who sought to revive Spanish art after the Civil War; he directed it until its dissolution in 1960. Saura is known for his expressionist-informalist works -- crucifixions, nudes, self-portraits and shrouds -- painted in an austere palette dominated by black, grey and white that echoes Goya, Velazquez and Picasso. His gestural brushwork and raw figuration made him one of Spain's most internationally recognised post-war artists, with retrospectives at the Guggenheim Bilbao and the Reina Sofia.
named_after: Antonio Saura

name: Álvarez de Villaamil
etymology_summary: Named after the street honouring Jenaro Perez Villaamil y Duguet (1807-1854), the great Spanish romantic landscape painter from Ferrol (Galicia). He introduced the landscape genre to Spanish painting and is best remembered for 'Espana artistica y monumental', a monumental three-volume collection of 122 lithographs of Spain's cities and monuments published in Paris (1842-1850) with texts by Patricio de la Escosura. Considered one of the most beautiful lithographed travel books of Spanish Romanticism, it documented Toledo, Seville, Burgos, Madrid and dozens of other sites. The Museo del Prado holds a celebrated diptych with 42 of his monumental views.
named_after: Jenaro Pérez Villaamil

name: Blasco Ibáñez
etymology_summary: Named after the street honouring Vicente Blasco Ibanez (1867-1928), Valencian novelist, journalist and Republican politician. His 1916 novel 'Los cuatro jinetes del Apocalipsis', set among Argentine expatriates in World War I, became a global bestseller and was adapted by Hollywood in 1921 in a Rex Ingram film that turned Rudolph Valentino into cinema's first sex symbol; its tango scene ignited a nationwide dance craze in the United States. 'Sangre y arena' was likewise filmed with Valentino in 1922. Blasco Ibanez was also elected to the Cortes six times and spent his final years in exile on the French Riviera, where he died in Menton.
named_after: Vicente Blasco Ibáñez

name: María Tudor
etymology_summary: Named after the street honouring Mary Tudor / Maria I of England (1516-1558), the first queen regnant of England. She was the only surviving child of Henry VIII and Catherine of Aragon -- herself daughter of the Reyes Catolicos, Ferdinand and Isabella -- giving Mary a direct link to the Spanish Crown. In 1554 she married the future Felipe II of Spain at Winchester Cathedral; the couple were proclaimed joint rulers of England, France, Naples, Jerusalem and Ireland. A crucial clause in the marriage treaty barred Felipe from being crowned king in his own right, safeguarding English sovereignty. Mary's reign saw a brief Catholic restoration before her death in 1558.
named_after: María I de Inglaterra

name: Palas de Rey
etymology_summary: Named after the street referencing Palas de Rei, a municipality in Lugo (Galicia) on the Camino Frances to Santiago de Compostela, about 65 km from the Cathedral. The name derives from Latin 'Palatium Regis' (Palace of the King), traditionally linked to Visigothic King Witiza (r. 702-710), who is said to have kept a palace here. According to chronicle tradition, it was in Palas that Witiza killed Duke Favila of Galicia, father of Don Pelayo, the future hero of the Reconquista. Witiza had come to Galicia around 701 fleeing plague and a Byzantine incursion; he was only fourteen when anointed king.
named_after: Palas de Rei

name: Las Tablas
etymology_summary: Named after the Las Tablas PAU (Programa de Actuacion Urbanistica), one of the large residential developments approved under Madrid's 1997 General Plan. 'Tablas' in its agricultural sense means flat, rectangular strips of cultivable land (RAE: 'faja de tierra de labor'), describing the open terrain of former farmland before urbanisation began in the early 2000s. The neighbourhood now houses the Distrito Telefonica campus (Distrito C), a 390,000 m2 corporate headquarters designed by Rafael de La-Hoz and inaugurated in 2008 for some 14,000 employees. This Metro Ligero ML1 station shares the name with the nearby metro Line 10 station but serves the light-rail route running from Pinar de Chamartin.
named_after: Las Tablas neighbourhood (tablas: flat terrain plots)

name: Colonia Jardín
etymology_summary: Named after the 'Colonia Jardin' (garden colony), a planned neighbourhood inspired by the English Garden City movement of Ebenezer Howard and the Linear City of Arturo Soria. These 'colonias' emerged around 1915-1924. Interchange with Metro line 10.
named_after: Colonia Jardín (garden city neighbourhood, early 20th-century urban planning model)

name: Prado de la Vega
etymology_summary: Named after the local area between Boadilla and Pozuelo. 'Prado' means 'meadow' (Latin pratum); 'de la Vega' means 'of the fertile plain'. Archaeological excavations along the Arroyo de la Vega uncovered 'La Vega', a small Visigoth settlement with thirteen rooms, as well as the nearby San Babiles hill necropolis (6th-8th c.). The station opened in 2007 on Metro Ligero line ML2 in what was once open agricultural floodplain.
named_after: Prado de la Vega (meadow of the fertile plain)
source: RAE (dle.rae.es/prado; dle.rae.es/vega); soloboadilla.es (Visigoth settlement 'La Vega'); es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Estacion_de_Prado_de_la_Vega;Ayto. Boadilla del Monte (ayuntamientoboadilladelmonte.org)

name: Colonia de los Ángeles
etymology_summary: Named after the Colonia de los Angeles, founded in 1926 when its owner parcelled the land as part of a wave of 'colonias de hotelitos' that transformed Pozuelo after the railway arrived in 1861. Madrid's bourgeoisie had discovered the area as a summer retreat, and colonies like San Jose (1914) and Los Angeles sprang up along the Camino de Humera. The Sociedad Colonia de los Angeles was formally created in 1929, and the first fiestas in honour of Nuestra Senora de los Angeles were celebrated in 1942. The colony retains its low-density garden character wedged between the Casa de Campo and Somosaguas.
named_after: Colonia de los Ángeles (neighbourhood near Cerro de los Ángeles)
source: asoclosangeles.org/colonia-los-angeles (founded 1926); pozuelodealarcon.org/tu-ayuntamiento/tu-ciudad/acerca-de-pozuelo/historia; archimadrid.org (patrona Nuestra Senora de los Angeles);Ayto. Boadilla del Monte (ayuntamientoboadilladelmonte.org)

name: Prado del Rey
etymology_summary: Named after the Prado del Rey area. 'Prado del Rey' means 'the King's Meadow' (from Latin pratum: meadow), indicating a royal meadow or pasture belonging to the Crown. The area was historically part of royal hunting grounds. The Arroyo Prado del Rey still flows through the area. The site later became the headquarters of RTVE (state television) from 1964, making 'Prado del Rey' synonymous with Spanish public broadcasting.
named_after: Prado del Rey (the King's Meadow, royal pastureland)
source: es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prado_del_Rey;Mesa del Arbol de Carabanchel (mesadelarbolcarabanchel.com);La Cerca (lacerca.com)

name: Somosaguas Sur
etymology_summary: Named after the Somosaguas area in Pozuelo de Alarcon. 'Somosaguas' is a compound of 'somo' (from Latin summum: the highest part, elevated area) + 'aguas' (waters), referring to elevated terrain with water sources. The area historically had ferruginous springs. The hamlet of San Juan de Somosaguas was depopulated during the fratricidal wars between Pedro I and Enrique II (14th century).
named_after: Somosaguas (elevated terrain with springs, from Latin summum + aguas)
source: Toponomasticon Hispaniae (toponhisp.org -- Somosierra cognate lists Somosaguas); pozuelodealarcon.org/tu-ayuntamiento/tu-ciudad/acerca-de-pozuelo/historia; elcorreodepozuelo.com (ferruginous springs); es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Somosaguas

name: Somosaguas Centro
etymology_summary: Named after central Somosaguas in Pozuelo de Alarcon. 'Somo' (Latin summum: summit) + 'aguas' (waters) describes elevated terrain with springs. The hamlet of San Juan de Somosaguas was depopulated during the 14th-century civil wars of Pedro I and Enrique II. From the mid-20th century the area became one of Madrid's most exclusive residential enclaves. On 1 Aug 1980 the Marquesses of Urquijo were murdered in their Somosaguas mansion -- a crime that remains one of Spain's great unsolved mysteries.
named_after: Somosaguas (elevated terrain with springs, from Latin summum + aguas)
source: Toponomasticon Hispaniae (toponhisp.org -- Somosierra cognate lists Somosaguas); pozuelodealarcon.org/tu-ayuntamiento/tu-ciudad/acerca-de-pozuelo/historia; elcorreodepozuelo.com (ferruginous springs); es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Somosaguas

name: Pozuelo Oeste
etymology_summary: Named for western Pozuelo de Alarcon. 'Pozuelo' derives from Latin 'puteolus' (diminutive of puteus: well), referencing abundant wells and water mines. First documented in 1208 when Alfonso VIII delimited borders between Segovia, Toledo, and Madrid. Originally 'Pozuelo de Aravaca' until 1632, when Gabriel de Ocana y Alarcon purchased the lordship and required his surname be added. From the 19th century a summer retreat for Madrid's bourgeoisie, it became one of Spain's wealthiest commuter towns from the 1970s. The station sits near the luxury urbanization La Finca.
named_after: Pozuelo de Alarcón west (Latin puteolu: small well/spring)

name: Bélgica
etymology_summary: Named after the Calle Belgica (Belgium). The street belongs to the Avenida de Europa zone in Pozuelo de Alarcon, where over thirty streets honour European nations and capitals: Francia and Paris, Alemania and Berlin, Inglaterra and Londres, Holanda and La Haya, Suiza and Berna, Austria and Viena, among others. The theme reflects the pro-European optimism of the 1980s-90s, when Spain had recently joined the EEC (1986) and Pozuelo was expanding rapidly. Nearby Calle Bruselas and Calle Estrasburgo nod to the seats of EU institutions.
named_after: Belgium
source: es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Estacion_de_Belgica_(Metro_Ligero); Ayto. Pozuelo de Alarcon (Callejero por Zonas CSV)

name: Dos Castillas
etymology_summary: Named after the Via de las Dos Castillas street. 'Dos Castillas' (Two Castiles) refers to the historical kingdoms of Castilla la Vieja (Old Castile, now Castilla y Leon) and Castilla la Nueva (New Castile, now Castilla-La Mancha). The distinction dates to the 13th century when the Reconquista pushed southward past the Sierra de Guadarrama. Madrid sits precisely on the boundary -- originally part of New Castile's Toledo kingdom. The street name reflects Pozuelo de Alarcon's location within this Castilian heartland.
named_after: Calle Dos Castillas (Two Castiles: Castile and León + Castile-La Mancha)

name: Campus de Somosaguas
etymology_summary: Named after the Complutense University campus built at Somosaguas in 1968 when the Franco regime deliberately relocated the combative Faculties of Economics and Political Sciences away from Ciudad Universitaria to isolate student anti-regime protests. 'Somosaguas' combines 'somo' (Latin 'summum': elevated ground) + 'aguas' (waters), describing hills with natural springs. The area historically had ferruginous mineral springs. The medieval hamlet of San Juan de Somosaguas was depopulated during the 14th-century wars between Pedro I and Enrique II.
named_after: Universidad Complutense de Madrid

name: Avenida de Europa
etymology_summary: Named after the Avenida de Europa (Avenue of Europe), the central boulevard of a zone in Pozuelo de Alarcon developed during the 1980s-90s residential boom that followed Spain's 1986 entry into the European Economic Community. The avenue lends its name to the surrounding neighbourhood, where more than thirty streets honour European countries and capitals from Andorra to Viena. Today it is one of Pozuelo's main commercial axes, lined with shops, restaurants, and a shopping centre.
named_after: Avenida de Europa (Pozuelo de Alarcón)

name: Berna
etymology_summary: Named after the Calle Berna (Bern), the Swiss federal capital. The street lies in the Avenida de Europa zone of Pozuelo de Alarcon, where over thirty streets carry a European geographic theme: Francia and Paris, Alemania and Berlin, Suiza and Berna, Inglaterra and Londres, Holanda and La Haya, plus Belgica, Dinamarca, Finlandia, Irlanda, Austria, Portugal, Grecia, and Monaco. The naming dates from the 1980s-90s expansion that transformed Pozuelo into one of Madrid's wealthiest suburbs. The pattern pairs each country with its capital, so Suiza and Berna sit side by side.
named_after: Bern

name: Estación de Aravaca
etymology_summary: Terminal station connecting to Cercanias. Named after the Aravaca district, documented since 1222 when Alfonso VIII's fuero organised Madrid's hinterland into three sexmos (rural tax districts): Aravaca, Villaverde, and Vallecas. The Sexmo de Aravaca grouped Pozuelo, Las Rozas, Majadahonda, Boadilla, Alcorcon, Leganes, and Carabanchel. Joaquin Caridad Arias (Anales del Instituto de Estudios Madrilenos, 2004) proposed a Celtic origin, linking the name to the Arevacos tribe documented by Pliny, whose name derived from the river Areva. Annexed to Madrid in 1951.
named_after: Aravaca
source: Joaquin Caridad Arias (Anales del Instituto de Estudios Madrilenos 44, 2004, pp. 821-830); es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aravaca_(Madrid)

name: Ciudad de la Imagen
etymology_summary: Named after the Ciudad de la Imagen (City of the Image) business park in Pozuelo de Alarcon, a complex specializing in audiovisual industries. Home to Telemadrid (the regional broadcaster), ECAM (Escuela de Cinematografia y del Audiovisual), the Filmoteca Espanola (national film archive), and dozens of production companies. The park was conceived in the early 1990s to create a Spanish 'media city' comparable to London's Soho or Hollywood's studio lots. Its proximity to the Ciudad del Cine (Kinepolis) and Jose Isbert stations creates a uniquely cinema-themed corridor on the ML3 line.
named_after: Ciudad de la Imagen (audiovisual business park in Pozuelo)

name: José Isbert
etymology_summary: Named after Jose Ysbert Alvarruiz 'Pepe Isbert' (1886-1966), legendary Spanish actor whose diminutive frame and unmistakable husky voice made him the face of mid-century Spanish cinema. He starred in two masterpieces by director Luis Garcia Berlanga: 'Bienvenido, Mister Marshall' (1953), in which he plays the endearingly deaf mayor of a small Castilian village preparing to impress visiting Americans, and 'El verdugo' (1963), a dark Berlanga-Azcona comedy about a reluctant executioner. Over decades he worked alongside Fernando Fernan Gomez, Jose Luis Lopez Vazquez and directors like Edgar Neville and Ladislao Vajda. The station sits near the Filmoteca Nacional in Ciudad de la Imagen.
named_after: José Isbert

name: Ciudad del Cine
etymology_summary: Named for its location in the Ciudad de la Imagen audiovisual park in Pozuelo de Alarcon. 'Ciudad del Cine' = 'City of Cinema'. The complex houses Kinepolis Madrid, a 25-screen Belgian multiplex opened in 1998 that won a Guinness record for the world's largest cinema (9200+ seats) and has hosted over 50 million visitors and 400 film premieres. Alongside it sit Telemadrid's headquarters, the ECAM film school (Escuela de Cinematografia y Audiovisual de la Comunidad de Madrid), the Television Academy's offices and the Filmoteca Espanola archive. The audiovisual-themed development transformed former farmland west of Madrid into Spain's most concentrated media production district.
named_after: Ciudad del Cine (Cinema City, Boadilla del Monte film facilities area)
source: es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Estacion_de_Ciudad_del_Cine;Ayto. Boadilla del Monte (ayuntamientoboadilladelmonte.org); es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ciudad_de_la_Imagen; elespanol.com (Kinepolis 25 anos); kinepolis.es

name: Cocheras
etymology_summary: Named after the Metro Ligero Oeste tram depot ('cocheras' = depots/garages) where the Citadis fleet is housed and maintained. 'Cochera' derives from 'coche' (carriage), which entered Spanish from Hungarian 'kocsi' via German 'Kutsche', after the town of Kocs where sprung carriages were invented in the 15th century. Madrid's original tramway network reached 188 km before being dismantled in 1972; the Metro Ligero, opened in 2007, marked the return of streetcar transit after a 35-year absence.
named_after: Cocheras (tram/light rail depot and maintenance facility)

name: Retamares
etymology_summary: Named after the Retamares area. From 'retama' (broom plant, from Arabic 'ratama') + collective suffix '-es', meaning 'place of broom bushes'. The area is dominated by the Base de Retamares, popularly nicknamed 'the Spanish Pentagon'. After NATO's Allied Force Command Madrid was deactivated in June 2013, Spain's Estado Mayor de la Defensa (Joint Chiefs of Staff) took over the facilities in 2014 and consolidated key commands here: the Operations Command, the Joint Cyber Command, the Armed Forces Intelligence Centre (CIFAS), and the Joint Special Operations Command. The Military School of Cyber Operations was founded on the base in 2023.
named_after: Retamares (retamar: place of broom plants, Retama sphaerocarpa)
source: RAE (dle.rae.es/retama -- Arabic ratama); etimologias.dechile.net/?retama; es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Estacion_de_Retamares; es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Base_de_Retamares; elconfidencialdigital.com (Retamares)

name: Montepríncipe
etymology_summary: Named after the Monte Principe residential urbanization. The land was part of the Monte de Boadilla, owned from 1761 by Infante Luis Antonio de Borbon. Through inheritance it passed to Carlota Luisa Godoy y Borbon, who married Camilo Ruspoli, Principe de Cerveteri. The Ruspoli family owned the estate until the 1960s-2000s. The name combines 'Monte' (the Boadilla woodland) with the princely title of its Ruspoli owners.
named_after: Montepríncipe (residential development, CEU San Pablo University campus)

name: Ventorro del Cano
etymology_summary: Named after the Ventorro del Cano area in Alcorcon. 'Ventorro' is a diminutive of 'venta' (inn/tavern from Latin vendita), a small roadside establishment for travelers. 'Del Cano' is the surname of the innkeeper. Historically a stopping point (parada de postas) on the old Camino de Extremadura, documented as existing until at least 1828.
named_after: Ventorro del Cano (Cano's roadside inn on the Camino de Extremadura)

name: Prado del Espino
etymology_summary: Named after the Prado del Espino area. 'Prado' means meadow and 'espino' refers to the common hawthorn (Crataegus monogyna), a thorny shrub native to Europe that each spring covers itself in fragrant white five-petalled flowers and in autumn bears bright red berries. The hawthorn once grew wild here before the land was developed. Since 2004 the site houses the Parque Empresarial Prado del Espino, a business park with around 150 companies and 2500 employees, adjacent to Santander's Ciudad Financiera. Its internal streets carry artisan-trade names: Artesanos, Forjadores, Impresores.
named_after: Prado del Espino (meadow of the hawthorn, from Latin pratum + spinus)

name: Cantabria
etymology_summary: Named after the Avenida de Cantabria. Cantabria is the northern Spanish coastal region whose ancient Cantabri resisted Rome so fiercely that Augustus himself took command in 29 BC. The avenue and nearby streets Altamira and Picos de Europa were named because Santander bank's massive Ciudad Financiera campus sits adjacent; the bank's origins in the city of Santander made Cantabrian landmarks the natural theme. Elsewhere in Boadilla, streets follow other motifs: rivers in Parque Boadilla, valleys in Las Lomas, islands in Valdepastores.
named_after: Cantabria
source: es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Estacion_de_Cantabria_(Metro_Ligero);Ayto. Boadilla del Monte (ayuntamientoboadilladelmonte.org); soloboadilla.es (Un recorrido por nuestro callejero)

name: Ferial de Boadilla
etymology_summary: Named after the recinto ferial (fairground) of Boadilla del Monte where the annual fiestas in honour of the Virgen del Rosario are held. 'Ferial' derives from Latin 'ferialis', related to 'feria' (fair/market day), originally meaning a day of rest or religious observance. Boadilla itself may trace its name to Arabic 'Boadil-la' -- archaeological finds of mosque foundations and possible Arab burials support pre-Reconquista settlement. Alternatively, the name may honour Beatriz de Boadilla, wife of Andres Cabrera who received the Chinchon lordship from the Reyes Catolicos.
named_after: Ferial de Boadilla (fairground/exhibition area of Boadilla del Monte)

name: Boadilla Centro
etymology_summary: Named for its central location in Boadilla del Monte. The municipality name has two competing etymologies per the Toponomasticon Hispaniae: (1) Germanic *buwitha (arch/vault), metaphorically applied to terrain; or (2) Latin *bovata (dehesa boyal, ox-grazing pasture), both yielding the diminutive 'Bobadilla' > 'Boadilla'. The earliest documentation is from the 1222 Fuero de Madrid. The Infante Luis Antonio de Borbon acquired the lordship in 1761 and commissioned the magnificent neoclassical palace designed by Ventura Rodriguez (1763-1765), now a cultural centre. The station is on Metro Ligero line ML3.
named_after: Boadilla del Monte

name: Nuevo Mundo
etymology_summary: Named after the Avenida Nuevo Mundo in Boadilla del Monte. 'Nuevo Mundo' = 'New World', part of an Americas/Age of Discovery naming theme in the municipality's streets: nearby stand Calle Cristobal Colon and other thoroughfares honouring conquistadors and navigators. Boadilla also displays historical naval artefacts -- including a cannon at the Colon-Victimas del Terrorismo intersection and an anchor from the ship Hernan Cortes at the Virgen del Carmen roundabout -- reinforcing the neighbourhood's connection to Spain's maritime past. The station serves a modern residential development on ML3 (Metro Ligero Oeste), opened in 2007.
named_after: Calle Nuevo Mundo (New World, Americas reference in Boadilla del Monte)
source: es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Estacion_de_Nuevo_Mundo_(Metro_Ligero);Ayto. Boadilla del Monte (ayuntamientoboadilladelmonte.org); boadilla-del-monte.callejero.net; eldebate.com/espana/madrid (tres objetos historicos Boadilla)

name: Siglo XXI
etymology_summary: Named after Calle Siglo XXI ('21st Century Street') in Boadilla del Monte. The futuristic name reflects a municipality that exploded from a small rural village into an affluent suburb of over 50,000 residents. In the 1980s Boadilla's growth pushed westward; by the 2000s, Siglo XXI represented the newest wave beyond the M-50 motorway. The ML3 Metro Ligero line opened in 2007, connecting these developments to Madrid via Colonia Jardin.
named_after: Siglo XXI development (21st Century, modern residential area in Boadilla)

name: Infante Don Luis
etymology_summary: Named after the Infante Luis Antonio de Borbon y Farnesio (1727-1785), youngest son of King Felipe V and brother of Carlos III. He acquired the lordship of Boadilla in 1761 and commissioned the neoclassical palace (1763-1765) designed by Ventura Rodriguez.
named_after: Luis Antonio de Borbón y Farnesio

name: Puerta de Boadilla
etymology_summary: Terminal station of the ML3 Metro Ligero line, opened 27 Jul 2007. 'Puerta de Boadilla' = 'Gateway to Boadilla del Monte', whose toponym derives from the Latin diminutive 'boveda/bovadilla' (small vault or arched bridge). The station sits at the Virgen de la Paz roundabout in the Siglo XXI neighbourhood. ML3 has reached a record of nearly 16,000 daily weekday users, reflecting Boadilla's transformation from a rural lordship into a commuter suburb of over 50,000.
named_after: Boadilla del Monte

name: Plaza de Toros
etymology_summary: Named after Parla's portable bullring, erected seasonally for the fiestas patronales. 'Plaza de toros' literally means 'square of bulls' though bullrings are circular; the term preserves the memory of when bullfights were held in rectangular town squares. Spain has over 1,700 bullrings -- more than any other single building type. Parla's is a temporary ring set up during festivities in honour of Nuestra Senora de la Asuncion, reflecting the strong taurine tradition in towns south of Madrid. The station marks the southern starting point of the Tranvia de Parla circular line.
named_after: Plaza de Toros de Parla (bullring)

name: Julio Romero de Torres
etymology_summary: Named after the street honouring Julio Romero de Torres (1874-1930), Spanish painter from Cordoba known for deeply Spanish symbolist art. Professor at the Real Academia de Bellas Artes de San Fernando.
named_after: Julio Romero de Torres

name: La Ballena
etymology_summary: Named after the La Ballena neighbourhood in Parla. The name derives from a popular legend: a large natural lagoon existed in northern Parla (now the 'La Laguna' neighbourhood), and a muleteer threw his 'albarda' (pack saddle) into the water, where it floated resembling a whale's back. Residents of Getafe came to 'fish the whale'. A folk copla mocks this event. The Parque de la Ballena (built 2000) features a giant metal whale tail sculpture. The whale has become one of Parla's municipal symbols.
named_after: La Ballena (folk legend of whale sighting in Parla's lagoon)
source: leyendasmundialesmagicas.blogspot.com/2017/12/una-ballena-parla-madrid.html; Raul Cordero 'La ciudad de la ballena'; esculturayarte.com/007314/Cola-de-Ballena-en-Parla.html; es.wikipedia.org/wiki/La_Ballena_(Parla)

name: Parla Centro-Bulevar Norte
etymology_summary: 'Parla Centro' indicates the town centre location. 'Bulevar Norte' refers to the northern boulevard. The municipality name has debated etymology: Roman anthroponym 'Parilus', Latin 'parabola' (speech), or folk legend of a mute woman who began to 'parlar'.
named_after: Parla town centre + Bulevar Norte (northern boulevard)

name: Iglesia Centro
etymology_summary: Named for its proximity to the Iglesia de Nuestra Senora de la Asuncion, Parla's parish church built in the early 16th century on the old Camino Real from Madrid to Toledo. Its oldest surviving element is a Gothic pentagonal apse in Toledan-style brick-and-stone masonry ('aparejo toledano'). The church replaced an earlier medieval 'Santa Maria de Parla'. Heavily restored in the 1920s and 1940s after deterioration, it received a new altarpiece in 2020 replicating the style of the original by the Renaissance master Juan de Borgona.
named_after: Iglesia de Nuestra Señora de la Asunción (Parla parish church)

name: Bulevar Sur-Miguel Ángel Blanco
etymology_summary: 'Bulevar Sur' means Southern Boulevard. Miguel Angel Blanco (1968-1997) was a 29-year-old People's Party councillor in Ermua (Basque Country) kidnapped by ETA on 10 July 1997. The terrorists issued a 48-hour ultimatum: transfer all ETA prisoners to Basque prisons or Blanco would die. During those two days six million Spaniards took to the streets in the largest demonstrations since the transition to democracy. Fifty minutes after the deadline, Blanco was found shot in the head. The unprecedented uprising became known as the 'Espiritu de Ermua' and marked a turning point against terrorism. Streets across Spain were named in his honour.
named_after: Miguel Ángel Blanco

name: Reyes Católicos
etymology_summary: Named after the Calle Reyes Catolicos, honouring Queen Isabel I of Castile (1451-1504) and King Fernando II of Aragon (1452-1516). Their 1469 marriage united Spain's two largest crowns, and their decade-long campaign ended with the conquest of Granada on 2 January 1492, closing nearly eight centuries of Muslim rule in Iberia. Pope Alexander VI granted them the title 'Reyes Catolicos' in 1496. Parla's historic centre names streets after Spanish monarchs; the adjacent tram stop is Isabel II. They also sponsored Columbus's first voyage that same year.
named_after: Reyes Católicos

name: Isabel II
etymology_summary: Named after the street honouring Queen Isabel II of Spain (1830-1904), who reigned 1833-1868. Under her reign Spain entered the railway age: the Madrid-Aranjuez line, the peninsula's second railway, was inaugurated on 9 February 1851 with the queen presiding. The royal train covered 50 km in 54 minutes, slashing a seven-hour stagecoach journey to under two hours. That line's terminus at Atocha still serves Cercanias passengers today. The street lies in Parla's historic centre, in a cluster of streets named after Spanish monarchs.
named_after: Isabel II de España

name: Parque Parla Este
etymology_summary: Named after the park in Parla Este, popularly called the 'Barrio del Universo' (Universe Neighbourhood), designed from 2001 with an astronomy-themed street grid unique in Spanish urbanism. All streets bear celestial names: Avenida de los Planetas, Avenida de las Estrellas, Calle Constelacion Andromeda, Calle Estrella Sirio, and many more. The neighbourhood's uniform blocks of up to 13 storeys were built rapidly to absorb Madrid's suburban growth, housing thousands of young families drawn south by affordable prices.
named_after: Parque Parla Este (eastern park of Parla)

name: Avenida Sistema Solar
etymology_summary: Named after the Avenida del Sistema Solar (Solar System Avenue), a main road in Parla Este. This neighbourhood, designed in 2001, is popularly known as the 'Barrio del Universo' because every street carries an astronomical name: the eight planets, stars such as Sirio, Vega, and Polar, the twelve zodiac constellations, and others like Orion, Pegaso, and Casiopea. Two grand avenues -- Avenida de las Estrellas and Avenida de los Planetas -- run north-south through the grid. The Solar System avenue frames them all as the overarching celestial structure.
named_after: Avenida del Sistema Solar (Solar System Avenue, astronomical theme in Parla Este)

name: Tierra
etymology_summary: Named after the Calle Tierra (Earth). The street is part of the astronomy-themed layout of Parla Este, a neighbourhood designed in 2001 and popularly known as the 'Barrio del Universo'. Every street evokes the cosmos: eight planets (Mercurio to Neptuno), stars (Sirio, Vega, Polar, Antares), zodiac constellations (Leo, Acuario, Libra), and others (Orion, Pegaso, Casiopea, Andromeda). The two main avenues are Avenida de las Estrellas and Avenida de los Planetas. Tierra sits at the third orbital position, just as Earth does in the solar system.
named_after: Planet Earth (astronomical theme in Parla Este Tranvía)

name: Venus
etymology_summary: Named after Calle Planeta Venus in Parla Este's 'Barrio del Universo', where the entire street grid follows an astronomical theme. Venus, named for the Roman goddess of love, is the brightest planet visible from Earth, appearing as the 'morning star' or 'evening star'. The planners arranged streets in rough orbital order from the Sun, with avenues like Sistema Solar, Estrellas, Planetas, and Galaxias as main arteries. This cosmic naming scheme is one of the most distinctive in the Madrid region. Dual station on the circular tram line.
named_after: Planet Venus (astronomical theme in Parla Este Tranvía)

name: Estrella Polar
etymology_summary: Named after Calle Estrella Polar in Parla Este's 'Barrio del Universo'. Polaris sits less than a degree from the celestial north pole, making it appear nearly motionless while all other stars rotate around it -- a guiding beacon for navigators since antiquity. In Parla Este's cosmic street grid, star names (Sirio, Antares, Polar) coexist with planet names and constellation names (Andromeda), forming one of Spain's most thematically coherent modern neighbourhoods. Dual station on the circular tram line.
named_after: Polaris / North Star (astronomical theme in Parla Este Tranvía)

name: Jaime I
etymology_summary: Named after Calle Jaime I. Jaime I 'el Conquistador' (1208-1276) was King of Aragon, Count of Barcelona, and Lord of Montpellier. He conquered Mallorca on 31 Dec 1229, then took Valencia on 28 Sep 1238, vastly expanding the Crown of Aragon across the Mediterranean. Beyond warfare, he codified the Valencian Furs (1261) and Aragonese Fueros (1247). Parla honours him among several streets named after Spanish monarchs.
named_after: Jaime I de Aragón

name: Polígono Industrial Ciudad de Parla
etymology_summary: Named after the Poligono Industrial Ciudad de Parla, developed by the state enterprise SEPES in the early 2000s. 'Poligono industrial' (from Greek 'polygonon': many-angled) is the standard Spanish term for a geometrically parcelled industrial estate. Parla's explosive growth from a village of around 2,000 in 1960 to over 130,000 today drove demand for industrial zones to provide local employment and reduce commuting to Madrid. The station is the last stop before the tram loops back toward the town centre.
named_after: Polígono Industrial Ciudad de Parla (Parla industrial estate)
